note: Erkundung im Berliner Bauarchiv (Kapitel 2, Konrad). Konrads Stimme: genau, längere Sätze, anfangs beschönigend, mit jedem Fund brüchiger. Alles bleibt in der fiktiven Welt von 1964; die reale Geschichte steht auf den Karten der Historiker (nur per Id verknüpft). Daten: data/explore/berlin.json.

strings.explore.berlin.porter.title: The porter
strings.explore.berlin.porter.text: Morning at the gate: frost, a suspended tram line, works on the axis – and a message from Hanna.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l1: Mornin’, Herr Adler! Minus fourteen at the Zoo, says the radio. In here it feels like minus fifteen.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l2: Good morning. So the heating is going according to plan.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l3: According to plan, yessir. The 74’s not running again, by the way. Closed as far as the axis, for the works on the Hall. Half the city’s on foot today.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l4: Those are scheduled expansion measures. The line will be clear again in the spring.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l5: Scheduled. Well, then. In my street they cleared out three houses, all scheduled-like. Since then it’s so quiet at night I can hear the Hall creak.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l6: That’s the frost. Steel and stone move when it gets cold.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l7: If you say so. Oh, and your sister rang yesterday. You’re to get in touch, about the flat.
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l8: Did she say what’s the matter with the flat?
strings.explore.berlin.porter.l9: Nope. Only that it’s urgent. And Frau Lenz’s little one is sitting on my stairs again. I ain’t seen nothing, if anyone asks.
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.title: Tea with Emil
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.text: Emil’s tea, a cactus that isn’t his, and a sign on the skirting board he wants nothing to do with.
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.l1: Herr Adler. Tea? It’s black, it’s hot, and it’s the only thing in this building that doesn’t get filed.
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.l2: Gladly. No sugar – I know there isn’t any.
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.l3: There is some. It’s reserved for the heads-of-department meeting. Like the coal.
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.l5: I’ve taken to watering the cactus of a colleague who’s gone away. Wednesdays. A thing like that needs surprisingly little. But not nothing.
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.l6: Gone away? We were told transferred.
strings.explore.berlin.emil_tea.l8: Drink up before it gets cold. And if you notice a sign down by the skirting board: that wasn’t me.
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.title: The librarian
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.text: A conversation about withdrawn books, the quarterly ‘clean-up’ and a register that doesn’t exist.
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l1: Herr Adler. You’re looking for something we haven’t got. One can tell by the way you stand in front of the shelves.
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l2: Volumes are missing from the holdings. Not lent out, not misplaced. They are simply missing.
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l3: They’ve been withdrawn. Every quarter a list comes from the ministry. ‘Clean-up’, it says on the envelope, typewritten.
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l4: And what happens to the books?
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l5: Pulped. They come back as paper. Perhaps you’ll write your next loan slip on a volume of poetry.
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l6: And the cards in the catalogue?
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l7: I pull them myself. And then I copy them out, for a register that doesn’t exist. Somebody has to know what’s missing.
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l8: Why are you telling me this?
strings.explore.berlin.librarian.l9: Because you’re the first today to ask. And because you’re a draughtsman. You know a gap can only be seen if you know the whole.
strings.explore.berlin.master_plan.title: The master plan
strings.explore.berlin.master_plan.text: The master plan of the North–South Axis, scale 1:5000, framed and as wide as a door; eight draughtsmen, six years, two of them mine. The axis runs through the city as if drawn with a ruler, and that is exactly what was done. By Tempelhof, a pencil circle: ‘Test load 1941 – settlement several times the permissible’. It was built all the same, on piles, driven deeper than ever before into Berlin’s sand. Sometimes I wonder whether it is all sinking. Less often do I wonder who drove the piles.
strings.explore.berlin.notice.title: Relocated
strings.explore.berlin.notice.text: A notice for the plan records office, ‘for updating the inventory plans’: names, house numbers, floors, each line followed by the word ‘relocated’ and a date from this autumn. The column ‘new address’ is empty throughout; presumably it will be filled in once the responsible office has completed its records. The list ends at Kolonnenstraße 12. My sister Hanna lives at number 14. I looked at the number until it stopped being a number.
strings.explore.berlin.pneumatic_tube.title: The capsule
strings.explore.berlin.pneumatic_tube.text: In the receiving basket of the pneumatic post lies a capsule addressed to ‘Dept. III – personal’. I don’t read other people’s post; the lid was only pushed on. Inside, a routing slip from the Registration Office: ‘Plan states South Axis, all revisions before state 4 – for culling. Urgent.’ Culling is an archive word; I have written it a hundred times. Today I am reading it for the first time. On an old slip in the same capsule someone has drawn a heart, and next to it: ‘5 p.m.?’ The pneumatic post carries whatever it is given.
strings.explore.berlin.clock.title: The regulator
strings.explore.berlin.clock.text: A regulator clock with a brass pendulum beside the gate, older than the building and, as the porter says, more reliable than any authority. It strikes the quarter-hours so softly that you only hear the last stroke. Every Monday the porter winds it and sets it by the time signal on the radio. Since the summer it has run three minutes fast all the same, and nobody reports it. Emil says it is the only clock in the building that dares anything.
strings.explore.berlin.card_catalogue.title: The gap at C-17
strings.explore.berlin.card_catalogue.text: The reading room’s card catalogue: oak drawers, brass labels, every card with shelf mark, location and loan note. Our catalogue does not lie; it merely falls silent in places. Between C-16, ‘Drainage, North Axis’, and C-18, ‘Lamp standards, type B’, there is a guide card with nothing behind it. On the tab: C-17. Beneath it, in pencil: ‘removed, see Dept. III’. No date, no initials. I would not have thought a gap in a card index could unsettle me so much.
strings.explore.berlin.reading_table.title: Reader 114
strings.explore.berlin.reading_table.text: On the reading table lies a pair of glasses, folded on a request slip. Reader 114 had ordered three volumes: a house chronicle of Schöneberg, the 1938 address book and a city map from 1936. Next to the reader number, in the lending desk’s green pencil: ‘Card withdrawn, 2 Nov.’ The glasses have been lying here for two days. Nobody clears them away. I think people are waiting for someone to collect them, knowing that nobody will come.
strings.explore.berlin.globe.title: A corrected world
strings.explore.berlin.globe.text: A globe from 1938, worn at the poles. The borders have since been redrawn in ink several times, by different hands and in different years; whole countries vanish under pasted-on strips of paper. A thin red line runs across the East: the Veltrava Line, March 1953. When you turn the globe it squeaks, and precisely where the line runs. I turned it twice to make sure.
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_1.title: A missing day
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_1.text: Shelf I, Administration: ministerial gazettes, schedules of responsibilities and the ‘Chronicle of the Reich Administration’, one volume per year, day by day, gilt-edged. I only meant to check when the axis was decided on, and got stuck in the 1942 volume. The 19th of January is followed by the 21st. No page cut out, no blacking out; the type runs smoothly over the place as if the day had never existed. I had never considered that days, too, can be culled.
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_2.title: The wooden volume
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_2.text: Shelf II, Reichsbahn: the timetable books, complete from 1934 to today, and beside them the service regulations in grey linen. One volume stands a finger’s breadth proud of the row: ‘Timetable orders – special trains – General Operating Directorate East – 1942–1944’. It is surprisingly light. It is a block of wood covered in linen, the spine neatly lettered so that the row looks complete. I know something about timetables: a train that is listed nowhere still runs. It just runs without witnesses.
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_3.title: Area to be cleared
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_3.prompt: Look at shelf III: Spatial planning
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_3.text: Shelf III, Spatial Planning. A large-format atlas, ‘The New Settlement in the East’, superbly printed. I recognise the hand of a very good draughtsman: clean hatching, villages on a grid, model farms at 1:500 with orchards. The legend knows only two colours. Green: ‘settlement area’. Grey: ‘area to be cleared’. On the grey lie towns whose names I cannot pronounce. Where the people who live there are to go is in no legend. I would have drawn it exactly the same way.
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_4.title: Omitted
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_4.text: Shelf IV, Public Health: building files of the province’s mental hospitals and care homes, grey folders that nobody else touches. A conversion plan from 1940: ward block II is to become a military hospital. Over the old floor plan, across a ward with eighty beds, a single word in red pencil: ‘omitted’. In our plans ‘omitted’ means: will not be built, will not be needed. I have written the word often. I had never seen it written over beds in which people lay.
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_5.title: Origin of materials
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_5.prompt: Look at shelf V: Labour deployment
strings.explore.berlin.lib_shelf_5.text: Shelf V, Labour Deployment: reports, statistics, decrees, and among them the commemorative volume for the inauguration in 1961, ‘The Great Hall – A Work of the People’. The photos show foremen, engineers, the minister with the trowel; the workers in the background are cut off at the edge of the picture. The appendix ‘Origin of Materials’ lists the granite works: Flossenbürg, Mauthausen, Groß-Rosen. I know the names from the delivery notes. I never asked who breaks the stone there.
strings.explore.berlin.lib_hidden.title: Brandt’s card
strings.explore.berlin.lib_hidden.text: The back panel of the bottom compartment of shelf V gives way. Behind it, a cavity, and in it an envelope with no sender and an index card in Brandt’s angular block capitals: “K., in case you’re looking: they don’t count rooms, they count addresses. Every flat we draw as ‘vacated’ has a card somewhere else. I asked where. Since then they’ve been asking about me. Water my cactus. – W. B., March 64”. The cactus on his windowsill is still alive. Someone is watering it, and it was not me.
strings.explore.berlin.mouse.title: Authorised personnel only
strings.explore.berlin.mouse.text: Down by the skirting board, where the plaster has crumbled away, a little sign is stuck on, hardly bigger than a postage stamp, typewritten: AUTHORISED PERSONNEL ONLY. Behind it, a hole the width of a thumb; in front of it, three breadcrumbs in a neat row and a thimbleful of water. Beneath, in pencil and very small: ‘Occupant: File’. She is presumably the only member of the archive’s staff who has never had to sign anything.
strings.explore.berlin.radio.title: A dot on the dial
strings.explore.berlin.radio.text: The radio in the porter’s lodge, built in 1955, its magic eye breathing green, tuned to the Reichssender as the house rules require. Beside the dial, a tiny pencil dot, far to the right, at a frequency that belongs to none of our stations. I did not check what plays there. I only checked very briefly: piano, double bass, brushes on a drum, someone laughing. Meanwhile the porter studied the stairs with great attention. The dot is not mine.
strings.explore.berlin.poster_aufbau.title: AUFBAU 1964
strings.explore.berlin.poster_aufbau.text: The poster of the year: the Great Hall as a white line drawing on midnight blue, the national emblem above it, and below it the figures every schoolchild knows: 290 metres high, a 250-metre dome, room for 180,000 people. The drawing comes from our department; I spent a year and a half on the window axes of the drum, and none of my drawings ever came back. The poster counts metres, seats and tonnes of granite. What it doesn’t count, I had not missed until today.
strings.explore.berlin.heater.title: Lukewarm
strings.explore.berlin.heater.text: The radiator in the reading room is the only one in the building that gets warm at all; the valve hisses, and something knocks in the pipes as if someone in the cellar were asking to be let in. Two small red mittens are drying on it. They belong to the daughter of Frau Lenz from the typing pool, who waits in the stairwell after school because children are not allowed in here. Everyone knows, nobody reports it. It is probably the only time our looking away does anyone any good.
strings.explore.berlin.pigeons.title: The committee
strings.explore.berlin.pigeons.text: Five pigeons sit on the window ledge, puffed up against the frost, in a row and facing the room, like a committee examining a proposal. One wears a ring on its leg; I have decided it means nothing. If you step up to the window they fly off and return a minute later, in the same seating order. The fat one on the far left looks as though it has reservations. I think it will be outvoted.
strings.explore.berlin.photo.title: After completion of the clearance
strings.explore.berlin.photo.text: The department’s chronicle beside the gate, 1938 to 1961, in three frames. In the last picture, July 1961, we stand in shirtsleeves in front of the model of the Hall, Professor Reinholt in the middle; on the mount: ‘After completion of the clearance’. I am in the second row, laughing. Someone has scratched out Herr Brandt’s face with a pin. We were told he had been transferred. Clearance means: flats whose tenants have moved out. Have been moved out.
strings.explore.berlin.coat_stand.title: A green scarf
strings.explore.berlin.coat_stand.text: On the coat stand hang Emil’s grey overall for the cellar, two umbrellas that refuse to belong to anyone, and a dark green woollen scarf. The scarf is Herr Brandt’s; it has hung there since March. Nobody takes it down, nobody takes it away. People just hang their own hats a little further to the left than they used to. I keep my coat on. In winter it is colder in the archive than in the street.
strings.explore.berlin.obs_brandt_desk.text: Brandt’s drawing table, under a sheet since March. Nobody has reassigned it, nobody has cleared it. On the windowsill beside it stands his cactus, the soil dark as if it had just been watered. You don’t reassign a desk until you are sure its owner won’t be coming back. Or as long as you don’t want to know.
strings.explore.berlin.radio_dial.title: A different station
strings.explore.berlin.radio_dial.text: I set the needle to the pencil dot, only to check that it was right. It was. After the piano came the news, in impeccable German: street names, clearances for the axis, a figure. The figure was higher than the one in our chronicle. I turned it back, exactly to the mark of the Reichssender. The porter kept his eyes on his newspaper the whole time. He did not turn a page.
